courses.title: The Commercial Spec: Writing Screenplays That Sell
courses.tagline: Learn how produced writers turn an idea into a marketable, producible feature spec.
courses.description: Most first screenplays fail not because the writer lacks talent but because the script was never designed for the marketplace. This course walks you through concept testing, logline engineering, genre contracts, budget-aware writing and the professional formatting expectations of readers at agencies, studios and production companies.
outcomes: Evaluate a premise for commercial viability before writing a page
Write a logline and one-page pitch that communicates genre, hook and stakes
Understand reader coverage and what 'Consider' vs 'Pass' actually means
Format a professional spec using industry-standard conventions

courses.title: Advanced TV Showrunner Masterclass
courses.tagline: Master pilot structure, series bibles, and running a professional writers' room.
courses.description: Television is a writer's medium. This masterclass dives deep into television architecture, episodic engines, franchiseable characters, pitch decks, and how to lead a writers' room with confidence.
outcomes: Architect a returning series pilot with an infinite episodic engine
Write a professional 15-page series bible and pitch deck
Break stories collaboratively in a simulated writers' room environment

lessons.title: What 'Commercial' Actually Means
lessons.content: Every studio, agency and production company employs readers whose job is to say no. A commercial script is not a 'dumb' script; it's a script where the promise of the premise is clear.

lessons.title: Coverage Walkthrough: Anatomy of a Pass
lessons.content: In this session we read real coverage on a spec that received a Pass and discuss the gap between intent and execution.

lessons.title: Genre Contracts and Audience Promises
lessons.content: When an audience buys a ticket to a heist film they are buying specific pleasures: assembling the crew, the plan, the twist.

lessons.title: The Irony Test
lessons.content: Blake Snyder called it irony; Craig Mazin calls it the central dramatic argument. A protagonist specifically ill-suited for the problem.

lessons.title: Building the One-Page Pitch
lessons.content: A one-page pitch is the document that gets you in the room. It is read in ninety seconds.

lessons.title: The Episodic Engine
lessons.content: An engine is the narrative machine that generates conflict episode after episode without exhausting the premise.

lessons.title: A/B/C Storylines in Drama
lessons.content: Balancing the serialized emotional arc with the procedural case of the week.

assignments.title: Logline & Irony Analysis
assignments.description: Submit 3 commercial loglines following the irony formula.
assignments.instructions: Include protagonist, flaw, goal, stakes, and ticking clock for each.

assignments.title: First 10 Pages Spec Opening
assignments.description: Write and submit the first 10 pages of your feature spec.
assignments.instructions: Must establish ordinary world, inciting incident, and tone by page 10.

assignments.title: Series Bible Pitch
assignments.description: Submit your 5-page series bible and pilot outline.
assignments.instructions: Must include logline, character bios, season 1 arc, and pilot teaser breakdown.

submissions.content:
Here is my logline submission:

1. When a blind hitman discovers his next target is his estranged daughter, he must protect her from the syndicate before they eliminate them both.
2. A corporate whistleblower is forced to spend 48 hours trapped in an elevator with the CEO she exposed.
3. An aging astronaut with severe memory loss must pilot the final shuttle home.

feedback.comments: Excellent work on these loglines, Alex! The first one has fantastic dramatic irony and high stakes. The second has great locked-room tension.
feedback.suggestions: Refine the third one to make the ticking clock more explicit.
